title: Prehistory and the Stone Age
summary: From fire through the spread of modern humans to the first farmers and villages: the Stone Age covers the longest stretch of human history.
overview: Prehistory is the period before the invention of writing. Since there are no written sources, we know about it only through bone finds, stone tools, cave paintings, settlement remains, and today also through the analysis of ancient DNA. The Stone Age is named after the most important material used for tools and is divided into the Paleolithic, the Mesolithic, and the Neolithic.

The ancestors of humans evolved in Africa. Early human forms such as Homo erectus learned to control fire and spread as far as Asia and Europe. Anatomically modern humans, Homo sapiens, emerged around 300,000 years ago in Africa. About 70,000 years ago small groups left the continent and, over the following tens of thousands of years, settled Asia, Australia, Europe, and finally the Americas.

The people of the Paleolithic lived as hunter-gatherers in small, mobile groups. They made tools from stone, bone, and wood, sewed clothing, buried their dead, and created works of art such as the cave paintings of Lascaux or small figures carved from ivory. For a time they shared Europe and Asia with other human species such as the Neanderthals, who died out about 40,000 years ago.

After the end of the last Ice Age, the Neolithic Revolution began around 11,500 years ago in the Fertile Crescent: people started to cultivate grain and to breed animals, and they settled down. This new way of life spread slowly into Europe, Africa, and Asia, and arose independently in China, the Americas, and other regions as well. Villages such as Çatalhöyük emerged, along with pottery, weaving, and larger buildings.

With settled life the population grew, stores were laid up, and possessions became more important. Towards the end of the Neolithic, the working of copper, the plough, and the wheel were added. Out of these innovations the first cities and early civilizations developed around 3500 BC in Mesopotamia and Egypt, and with them begins the history recorded in writing.
consequences: Modern humans spread out from Africa to settle every habitable continent and are today the only surviving human species.
The Neolithic Revolution turned hunter-gatherers into settled farmers and thereby created the basis for villages, cities, and states.
Farming and animal husbandry made storage, population growth, and the division of labour possible, but also inequality, property, and new diseases.
Tools, fire, language, art, and religion from the Stone Age remain among the fundamental features of human culture to this day.
Inventions such as pottery, weaving, the wheel, and metalworking paved the way for the early civilizations of the Bronze Age.
keyFacts: Around 2.6 million years ago early humans in East Africa make the first stone tools (Oldowan).
About 1.8 million years ago Homo erectus becomes the first human species to leave Africa, reaching Asia and Europe.
By 400,000 years ago at the latest, humans use fire regularly; around 300,000 years ago Homo sapiens emerges in Africa.
About 75,000 years ago the oldest known ornaments and decorative beads are produced in Blombos Cave in South Africa.
Around 50,000 years ago humans reach Australia and about 15,000 years ago the Americas; around 1500 BC the settlement of the Pacific islands begins.
From about 9500 BC the Neolithic Revolution begins in the Fertile Crescent, with farming, animal husbandry, and permanent villages such as Jericho.
Around 5000 BC copper working begins; around 3500 BC the wheel, the plough, and the domesticated horse are added.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: For hundreds of thousands of years people lived in small groups of mostly 20 to 50 individuals in which there were no fixed rulers. Decisions were probably made jointly, and standing rested on experience, success in hunting, or knowledge of plants and remedies. Since hunter-gatherers could carry hardly any possessions with them, differences between people remained small. Archaeology therefore speaks of largely egalitarian societies.

With settled life this changed. Stores, fields, herds, and houses could be inherited, and settlements such as Jericho or Çatalhöyük needed rules for water, land, and defence. In the Neolithic, richly furnished graves appear for the first time, showing that individual families had more influence and property than others. Communal structures such as stone circles, burial mounds, or town walls presupposed that someone was able to organize hundreds of people.

Towards the end of the Neolithic and in the Copper Age this development intensified. Copper axes, jewellery, and weapons from graves such as the one at Varna in Bulgaria marked rank and power. Village heads and clan leaders became chieftains, and chiefdoms eventually became the first cities and states of Mesopotamia and Egypt.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Everyday life in the Paleolithic was shaped by movement: groups followed animal herds, ripening fruit, and the seasons, and lived in caves, under rock shelters, or in tents made of hides and mammoth bones. Women and men shared the work, and gathering plants, nuts, eggs, and small animals often supplied more food than big-game hunting. Children learned by imitation; the old passed on knowledge about tools, paths, and stories.

Finds of healed bone fractures and of people in need of care show that the sick and injured were looked after. The dead were buried, often sprinkled with ochre and provided with jewellery or tools, which points to ideas of a life after death. Clothing made of hides was sewn with bone needles; sewing needles are attested from around 40,000 years ago.

In the villages of the Neolithic people lived closer together than ever before. Farming meant hard, monotonous work, and skeletons show more wear, tooth decay, and deficiency diseases than among hunter-gatherers. At the same time the number of children rose, because grain porridge shortened the period of breastfeeding. Diseases such as measles or tuberculosis passed from livestock to humans, and stores aroused the envy of neighbours, so that palisades and ditches were built around the villages.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: Symbolic thinking is older than previously assumed: in Blombos Cave in South Africa, people carved patterns into pieces of ochre 75,000 years ago and made beads from snail shells. In Europe, around 40,000 years ago, the ivory figures of the Swabian Jura were created, among them the Lion Man and the Venus of Hohle Fels, as well as flutes made from bird bones, the oldest known musical instruments.

Cave paintings such as those at Chauvet, Lascaux, or Altamira show mainly animals and rarely humans. Scholarship interprets them as part of hunting magic, initiation rites, or shamanism, but this is not certain. Burials with grave goods, animal figures, and the cult buildings of Göbekli Tepe point to ideas of spirits, ancestors, and supernatural forces long before the first temples were built.

The knowledge of Stone Age people was practical and extensive: they knew the properties of hundreds of plants, could strike flint with precision, boil adhesive from birch tar, and use the stars for orientation. Megalithic monuments such as Stonehenge or Newgrange are aligned to the solstices and show that the people of the Neolithic observed the course of the year closely. The invention of pottery made it possible to cook and store food, and its decoration today reveals to archaeologists the origin and contacts of the groups.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The technology of the Paleolithic developed slowly but steadily: from the simple flakes of the Oldowan through the bifacially worked hand axe of Homo erectus to the fine blades, spear-throwers, harpoons, and bows of Homo sapiens. Every innovation made hunting and food preparation more efficient. Trade already existed as well: shells and obsidian were exchanged over hundreds of kilometres.

With farming and animal husbandry an economy arose that could build up stores and produce surpluses. Grain was harvested with flint sickles, stored in granaries, and ground with grinding stones. Sheep and goats supplied milk, wool, and meat, and cattle later pulled the plough. From about 6000 BC irrigation canals in Mesopotamia made even dry areas fertile and allowed for larger villages.

In the Copper Age people began to smelt ores and cast metal in moulds. Copper axes, needles, and jewellery were sought-after goods for exchange, but still soft; only bronze solved this problem. The wheel and the cart, the potter's wheel, the loom, and domesticated horses and donkeys changed transport and craft and initiated the transition to the early civilizations.

title: Early Civilizations
summary: On the Euphrates, the Nile, the Indus, and the Yellow River the first cities, states, and scripts emerge: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus civilization, and China shape the Bronze Age.
overview: Around 3500 BC the first cities in the world emerged in Mesopotamia between the Euphrates and the Tigris. Irrigation agriculture produced surpluses that fed priests, craftsmen, merchants, and officials. In order to administer stores, dues, and trade, the Sumerians developed cuneiform. Temples and palaces, kings, laws, and standing armies characterize these early states.

On the Nile, around 3100 BC, a king from Upper Egypt united the land into a single kingdom. The pharaohs were regarded as gods on earth and had themselves buried in enormous pyramids. The annual Nile flood made Egypt a rich agricultural land whose culture, with hieroglyphs, mummification, and temple building, remained remarkably stable for almost three millennia.

Early civilizations arose in other river valleys as well: in the Indus Valley, around 2500 BC, systematically planned cities such as Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa flourished, with sewerage and standardized measures. In China the Shang dynasty ruled from about 1600 BC, and Chinese writing emerged from its oracle bones. In Mesoamerica the Olmecs laid the foundations of later cultures such as the Maya from 1200 BC onwards.

Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, gave the epoch its name. It made better weapons and tools possible and promoted long-distance trade, since tin was rare. Rulers such as Sargon of Akkad, Hammurabi of Babylon, or Ramesses II of Egypt created great empires, concluded alliances, and waged wars over trade routes and tribute. The treaty between the Egyptians and the Hittites after the Battle of Kadesh is the oldest surviving peace treaty.

Around 1200 BC many empires of the eastern Mediterranean collapsed within a few decades. Droughts, earthquakes, revolts, and attacks by the so-called Sea Peoples contributed to this. With the end of the Bronze Age the Iron Age began, in which new peoples such as the Phoenicians, Israelites, Assyrians, and Greeks determined the course of history.
consequences: With writing, history proper begins: administration, laws, literature, and knowledge could now be recorded permanently.
Cities, states, kings, officials, taxes, and armies arose in this period and shape political order to this day.
Collections of laws such as the Code of Hammurabi established the idea that law should be set down in writing and publicly known.
The astronomy, mathematics, calendars, medicine, and architecture of the early civilizations were taken over by the Greeks, the Romans, and later cultures.
The scripts of Egypt, Mesopotamia, and China became the forerunners of the alphabets and writing systems used worldwide today.
keyFacts: Around 3200 BC cuneiform emerges in Uruk; around 3100 BC a pharaoh unites Upper and Lower Egypt.
Around 2600 BC city-states such as Ur, Uruk, Lagash, and Kish compete in Sumer; their kings lie with rich grave goods in the Royal Tombs of Ur.
The Epic of Gilgamesh, transmitted on clay tablets from about 2100 BC, is humanity's oldest great work of literature.
Between 2000 and 1200 BC the palaces of the Minoans on Crete and of the Mycenaeans in Greece flourish, the first early civilizations of Europe.
From about 1650 BC the Hittites rule Anatolia from Hattusa and become Egypt's great rival.
Around 1200 BC many empires collapse; afterwards iron and the Phoenician alphabet of 22 letters come into general use.
From about 900 BC new powers emerge: the Neo-Assyrian Empire, the Kingdom of Kush in Nubia, and the Chavín culture in Peru.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The kings of the early civilizations derived their power from the gods. In Sumer the ruler was regarded as the deputy of the city god, to whom the temple and a large part of the land belonged; the pharaoh of Egypt was himself venerated as a god on earth, as the son of the sun god Ra and the embodiment of Horus. This religious justification made rule stable, but it also obliged the king to secure order, justice, and fertility.

Out of the city-states of Sumer, which fought each other over water and border land, territorial empires arose under Sargon of Akkad and later Hammurabi of Babylon, with governors, messengers, and tax lists. Administration rested on writing: scribes recorded harvests, dues, workers, and rations on thousands of clay tablets. In Egypt a vizier directed the officials of the provinces on behalf of the pharaoh, and in the Middle Kingdom a broad class of educated administrative officials emerged.

In the 2nd millennium BC a system of states took shape, made up of great powers such as Egypt, the Hittites, Babylon, Mitanni, and Assyria, which dealt with one another through envoys, letters in the Akkadian language, gifts, and marriage alliances. The Amarna letters and the treaty between Ramesses II and Hattusili III attest to this early diplomacy. After the collapse around 1200 BC, the Assyrians, using deportations, provinces, and a standing army, established the first empire to rule the entire Near East.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The societies of the early civilizations were strictly ordered. At the top stood the king, the priests, and high officials, below them scribes, merchants, and craftsmen; the great majority were peasants who worked the land of the temples, palaces, or large landowners and paid dues. Slaves, mostly prisoners of war or debtors, stood at the very bottom, but played a smaller role in the economy than they later did in Greece and Rome.

Women in Egypt had comparatively many rights: they could own property, conclude contracts, bring suits in court, and engage in trade. Individual women such as Hatshepsut even ruled as pharaoh, Nefertiti and Fu Hao exercised great influence, and Enheduanna led an important temple as high priestess. In Mesopotamia the Code of Hammurabi regulated marriage, dowry, divorce, and inheritance in detail; women of the upper class could work as priestesses or businesswomen, but were subordinate to their father or husband.

Everyday life for the majority took place in mudbrick houses with an inner courtyard. People ate bread, onions, lentils, dates, and fish, drank beer brewed from barley, and wine was a luxury. Children of the upper class spent years learning cuneiform or hieroglyphs in scribal schools, while peasant children helped in the fields. Festivals in honour of the gods, such as the New Year festival in Babylon or the Opet festival in Thebes, interrupted the working year and brought the whole city together.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The religions of the early civilizations knew many gods, who were responsible for natural forces, cities, and areas of life: Enlil, Inanna, and Marduk in Mesopotamia, Ra, Osiris, and Isis in Egypt, the weather god among the Hittites. Temples such as the ziggurat of Ur or the temple of Karnak were at once the dwelling of the gods, an economic enterprise, and a centre of learning. The Egyptians believed in a continued life after death, which required mummification, grave goods, and the judgement of the dead before Osiris.

With writing, literature came into being. The Epic of Gilgamesh tells of friendship, the fear of death, and a great flood; Egyptian texts such as the Story of Sinuhe, love songs, and wisdom teachings were copied out over centuries. Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon, composed hymns and is the first author known by name in the world. Around 1050 BC the Phoenicians simplified writing into an alphabet of 22 consonant signs, which the Greeks, the Romans, and later almost the entire world adopted.

The science of the early civilizations arose out of practical needs. Babylonian priests observed the stars and planets, predicted lunar eclipses, and created the division of the circle into 360 degrees and of the hour into 60 minutes. Egyptian physicians described wounds and remedies in papyri, surveyors recalculated the fields after every Nile flood, and the Egyptian calendar of 365 days became the model for our own.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The basis of the early civilizations was an agriculture that, thanks to irrigation and river silt, produced high surpluses. In Mesopotamia the canals had to be maintained constantly, because salinization threatened the fields; in Egypt the Nile flood governed the rhythm of sowing and harvest. The plough, the sickle, the donkey, and cattle, and in the Middle Kingdom also water-lifting devices and the Fayum project for reclaiming land, increased yields.

Bronze, made of copper and tin, was the decisive material for weapons, tools, and cult vessels, yet tin was rare and came from Anatolia, Iran, or Afghanistan. Trade routes therefore stretched over thousands of kilometres: lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, cedar wood from Lebanon, gold and ivory from Nubia, copper from Cyprus. The Uluburun shipwreck off the Turkish coast, dating from around 1300 BC, carried goods from at least seven regions.

Long-distance trade lay in the hands of merchants such as the Assyrians, who ran trading colonies in Anatolia, or the Phoenicians, who sailed the entire Mediterranean with their ships and founded colonies such as Carthage. Payment was made in weighed silver, grain, or copper; coins did not yet exist. After 1200 BC iron came into general use; it was more laborious to smelt, but its ore occurred almost everywhere and made tools and weapons affordable for many.

title: Ancient Greece and the Hellenistic Age
summary: Democracy, philosophy, theatre, and the Olympic Games arise in the Greek city-states; Alexander the Great carries Greek culture as far as Egypt and India.
overview: After the dark centuries that followed the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, hundreds of independent city-states, the poleis, emerged in Greece from about 800 BC. The Greeks adopted the alphabet from the Phoenicians, founded colonies all around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, and were bound together by a shared consciousness through language, gods, the epics of Homer, and the Olympic Games.

In Athens, through the reforms of Solon and Cleisthenes, a democracy developed in which the assembly of all male citizens made the most important decisions. Sparta, by contrast, was a military state under two kings. In the Persian Wars the Greeks repelled two attacks by the Persian Empire at Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea, which made Athens the leading sea power.

Under Pericles, Athens experienced a cultural flowering in the 5th century BC, with the building of the Acropolis, the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, the historical writing of Herodotus and Thucydides, and the philosophy of Socrates. The rivalry between Athens and Sparta led to the Peloponnesian War, which ended in 404 BC with the defeat of Athens and permanently weakened the Greek city-states.

In the 4th century BC Plato and Aristotle founded schools in Athens that shaped European philosophy and science. Politically, Macedonia rose to predominance under Philip II. His son Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire between 334 and 323 BC and pushed as far as Egypt and India. His early death left behind an empire that his generals divided among themselves.

In the Hellenistic age Greek and oriental culture merged. Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean, and Alexandria with its library became the centre of scholarship. One after another Rome subjugated the Hellenistic kingdoms; in 146 BC Greece became Roman, and with the death of Cleopatra in 30 BC Egypt was the last to fall to Rome.
consequences: Athenian democracy is the first known example of rule by the people and the point of reference for all modern democracies.
The philosophy, logic, mathematics, medicine, and historical writing of the Greeks form the foundation of European science.
Greek theatre, epic, lyric poetry, and sculpture set standards by which art and literature are still guided today.
Through Alexander's conquests and the Hellenistic age, the Greek language and culture spread as far as Egypt, Persia, and India; the New Testament was written in Greek.
The Romans took over Greek education, art, and the world of the gods and passed them on to medieval and modern Europe.
keyFacts: Between 750 and 550 BC Greek cities found hundreds of colonies from Spain to the Black Sea.
In 594 BC Solon reforms Athens and abolishes debt bondage; in 508 BC Cleisthenes lays the foundation of democracy.
In 480 BC Leonidas and 300 Spartans fall at Thermopylae; in the same year the Greeks win at Salamis.
In 472 BC The Persians by Aeschylus, the oldest surviving tragedy, is performed; in 447 BC construction of the Parthenon begins.
Around 400 BC Hippocrates and his school on Kos establish medicine as a science with natural causes.
In 331 BC Alexander founds Alexandria; after his death in 323 BC the Diadochi divide his empire in wars lasting until 281 BC.
In 212 BC Archimedes dies during the capture of Syracuse by the Romans; the science of the Hellenistic age lives on in Alexandria.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The Greek polis knew almost all the forms of government that political theory later described: kingship, aristocracy, tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy. In the 7th and 6th centuries BC tyrants seized power in many cities, often with the support of the people against the nobility; in Athens, Peisistratus and his sons promoted festivals, buildings, and farmers until Hippias was driven out in 510 BC. The word tyrant acquired its negative ring only later.

Athenian democracy rested on the popular assembly, which decided on war, peace, laws, and finances, on the Council of 500 filled by lot, and on jury courts with hundreds of judges. Almost all offices were allotted and filled anew each year; only the ten generals were elected, which is why Pericles directed policy through that office for decades. Women, slaves, and the numerous immigrants, the metics, remained excluded; citizens made up about one tenth of the inhabitants.

Sparta, by contrast, was governed by two kings, a council of elders, and five ephors elected annually; the full citizens lived as professional warriors off the land, which was worked by the unfree helots. After the Peloponnesian War, Sparta, Thebes, and Athens alternated as the leading power until Philip II of Macedonia subjugated the Greeks at Chaeronea in 338 BC. In the Hellenistic age kings such as the Ptolemies and the Seleucids ruled over vast empires, while the poleis retained only limited self-government.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The life of an Athenian family took place in a simple house with an inner courtyard; the men spent the day in the agora, in the gymnasion, or in the popular assembly, while the women of the citizen class ran the household, wove, and left the house mainly for religious festivals. Girls were married off at about 15 years of age, and boys learned reading, writing, music, and sport. In Sparta, by contrast, girls were trained physically, and women could own land.

Without slaves the Greek economy would have been inconceivable: they worked in households, workshops, in the fields, and under cruel conditions in the silver mines of Laurion, from which Athens financed its fleet. The symposion, the men's drinking party with conversation, songs, and games, was the centre of social life; hospitality was regarded as a sacred duty. Women such as Sappho on Lesbos or the educated Aspasia in Athens show that there were exceptions to the male-dominated order as well.

Sport and competition ran through Greek culture. Besides Olympia there were the games at Delphi, Corinth, and Nemea; victors were celebrated like heroes in their home cities and praised by poets such as Pindar. Theatre performances, music, and rhetoric were also competitions. The agon, the contest, shaped the idea that a person should distinguish himself through achievement.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The Greeks venerated Zeus, Athena, Apollo, and the other Olympians with sacrifices, processions, and festivals; every polis had its patron deity, and the temples on the Acropolis or at Delphi were magnificent buildings of marble. Cities and kings consulted the oracle of Delphi before wars and the founding of colonies; its ambiguous answers became proverbial. Mystery cults such as the one at Eleusis promised initiates a better life after death.

Out of the festivals of Dionysus, theatre arose in Athens: tragedies by Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides dealt with guilt, fate, and justice before thousands of spectators, while the comedies of Aristophanes mocked politicians and philosophers. Herodotus founded historical writing by asking after the causes of the Persian Wars, and Thucydides turned it into a critical analysis of power. The sculptors Phidias, Polykleitos, and Praxiteles created the ideal of the human body that Rome and the Renaissance took over.

From the 6th century BC the natural philosophers of Ionia sought natural explanations of the world instead of divine ones. Pythagoras and Euclid created mathematics based on proof, Hippocrates medicine, Aristotle biology and logic. In Alexandria, Eratosthenes calculated the circumference of the earth, Aristarchus supposed that the earth orbits the sun, and Archimedes discovered the laws of the lever and of buoyancy. This science was passed on to the Middle Ages through Byzantium and the Arab world.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: Mountainous, barren Greece fed its inhabitants with barley, olives, wine, and goats only with difficulty; shortage of land drove many cities to found colonies and to import grain from Sicily, Egypt, and the Black Sea region. In return Athens exported olive oil, wine, silver, and the painted vases of its pottery workshops, which today stand in all the great museums.

Around 600 BC the Greeks adopted the coin from Lydia and spread it across the entire Mediterranean; the Athenian silver owl became the most important trading currency. The harbour of Piraeus was the largest trading hub of the Aegean, with banks, warehouses, and shipyards. The triremes, warships with three banks of oars and 170 rowers, secured maritime trade and the power of Athens.

In the Hellenistic age cities such as Alexandria, Antioch, and Pergamon grew into metropolises with hundreds of thousands of inhabitants, planned street grids, water pipes, and libraries. Engineers developed catapults, cranes, the Archimedes screw for raising water, and forerunners of the steam engine, which however remained curiosities. The lighthouse of Pharos, one of the Seven Wonders of the World, showed ships the way into the harbour of Alexandria, through which grain from the Nile delta reached the whole Mediterranean world.

title: The Roman Empire
summary: From a small city on the Tiber to a world empire around the Mediterranean: Rome shaped the law, language, urban planning, and politics of Europe for centuries.
overview: According to legend, Rome was founded by Romulus in 753 BC. In fact the city grew out of several villages on the hills by the Tiber and was at first governed by kings. Around 509 BC the Romans drove out their last king and established a republic in which annually elected consuls, the Senate, and the popular assemblies shared power.

In the following centuries Rome subjugated first Italy and then, in the Punic Wars against Carthage, the western Mediterranean. Greece, Asia Minor, Gaul, and Egypt followed. The conquests brought enormous wealth, but also social tensions: smallholders were impoverished, slaves worked on large estates, and ambitious generals such as Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar used their legions for their own ends.

After civil wars and the murder of Caesar, his adoptive son Octavian established the principate as Augustus from 27 BC: formally the republic continued to exist, but in fact an emperor ruled. The Pax Romana of the first two centuries AD brought peace, trade, roads, aqueducts, and flourishing cities from Britain to Syria.

From the 3rd century onwards the empire fell into a crisis of civil wars, inflation, and attacks on the frontiers. Diocletian and Constantine reformed the administration and the army; Constantine promoted Christianity, which became the state religion in 380. In 395 the empire was finally divided into a western and an eastern half.

The Western Roman Empire disintegrated under the pressure of the migration of peoples. In 476 the Germanic military leader Odoacer deposed the last Western Roman emperor, Romulus Augustulus. The Eastern Roman Empire with its capital Constantinople continued to exist as Byzantium for almost another thousand years.
consequences: Roman law forms the basis of many European legal systems to this day.
Out of Latin arose the Romance languages Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Romanian; Latin terms shape science and the church.
Roads, cities, aqueducts, and building forms such as the arch, the dome, and concrete permanently influenced the architecture and infrastructure of Europe.
Christianity spread throughout the Roman Empire and became the defining religion of Europe.
The idea of a Roman imperial office lived on in the Holy Roman Empire and in the titles emperor and tsar.
keyFacts: Around 450 BC Roman law is set down in writing for the first time in the Twelve Tables.
From 73 to 71 BC the slave revolt of Spartacus shakes Italy; in 31 BC the naval battle of Actium decides the civil war in Octavian's favour.
In AD 80 the Colosseum is opened; under Trajan the empire reaches its greatest extent in 117, from Britain to Mesopotamia.
In 212 the emperor Caracalla grants Roman citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire through the Constitutio Antoniniana.
From 235 to 284 the empire experiences the Crisis of the Third Century, with more than 20 emperors, civil wars, and inflation; Diocletian reorganizes it from 284.
In 325 the Council of Nicaea under Constantine lays down the foundations of the Christian creed.
In 410 the Visigoths under Alaric sack Rome, in 451 Attila's Huns are stopped at the Catalaunian Plains, and in 476 the Western Roman Empire comes to an end.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The constitution of the republic rested on the distribution of power among magistrates who changed annually, the Senate as the council of former officeholders, and the popular assemblies. The Conflict of the Orders between the aristocratic patricians and the plebeians led over two centuries to the Twelve Tables, to the tribunes of the people with their right of veto, and finally to the opening of all offices. Abroad, Rome bound the defeated cities of Italy to itself through graded alliances and citizenship rights and was thus able to draw on enormous reserves of troops.

The conquest of the Mediterranean world overtaxed the institutions of a city republic. Governors enriched themselves in the provinces, generals such as Marius, Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar commanded armies that were personally loyal to them, and politics was determined by violence, bribery, and civil wars. The principate of Augustus solved the problem by concentrating power over the army and the provinces in one hand while at the same time preserving the Senate and republican forms.

The imperial period knew no fixed law of succession, which is why adoption, the army, and the Praetorian Guard decided who followed. In the 2nd century the adoptive emperors from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius brought stability; in the 3rd century the legions proclaimed dozens of soldier emperors. Diocletian divided rule among four rulers in the tetrarchy, introduced the court ceremonial of oriental kings, and founded the dominate, in which the emperor appeared as lord and god. Constantine and his successors joined this form of rule to Christianity.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Roman society was strictly graded: senators, equestrians, free citizens, freedmen, and slaves. The family stood under the almost unlimited authority of the father of the house, yet Roman women could own property, obtain a divorce, and, like Livia or Agrippina, exercise considerable influence at the imperial court. The system of clientage bound wealthy patrons and their clients together in a network of protection and allegiance.

In the Italy of the late republic slaves made up a third of the population; they toiled on country estates, in mines, and in households, but were also physicians, teachers, and administrators. Revolts such as that of Spartacus were put down with the utmost severity, yet slaves could also be freed and their children obtain citizenship. In 212 the Constitutio Antoniniana made almost all free inhabitants of the empire Romans.

Life in Rome, a city of a million people, took place in cramped tenement blocks, in markets, in the baths, and at the games. Free grain and entertainment, bread and circuses, secured the quiescence of the masses; in the Colosseum gladiators and animals died before 50,000 spectators, and in the Circus Maximus hundreds of thousands thrilled to chariot races. The provincial cities from Britain to Syria imitated the model of Rome with a forum, temples, a theatre, and baths, as Pompeii shows.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The Romans adopted the Greek gods under Latin names and supplemented them with deities of their own such as Janus and the household gods. Religion was a matter of state: colleges of priests, sacrifices, and omens accompanied every political act, and the imperial cult bound the provinces to Rome. Alongside this, mystery cults from the East spread, such as the worship of Isis and of Mithras, and from Judaea came Christianity, which survived the persecutions under Nero, Decius, and Diocletian and rose to become the state religion in the 4th century.

In literature and philosophy the Romans followed Greek models and yet created something of their own: Virgil's Aeneid as a national epic, the odes of Horace, the historical works of Livy and Tacitus, the satires of Juvenal. Stoicism shaped Roman ideas of duty and composure; Seneca and the emperor Marcus Aurelius left behind philosophical writings that are still read today. The Council of Nicaea in 325 showed how theology became an affair of the empire.

Rome's real achievement lay in law and organization. Jurists such as Gaius and Ulpian developed civil law into a system that the emperor Justinian had codified in the 6th century and whose influence continues to this day. Education rested on grammar and rhetoric; in Alexandria scholars such as the mathematician Hypatia were still active in late antiquity, and her murder in 415 announced the end of ancient science.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The Mediterranean was the Mare Nostrum, our sea, across which grain from Egypt and North Africa, oil from Spain, wine from Italy and Gaul, marble from Greece, and luxury goods from India and China flowed to Rome. The harbour of Ostia and the state-organized grain supply fed the capital. A uniform currency, safe sea routes after the destruction of the pirates by Pompey, and a legal system for contracts made the empire into an enormous economic area.

Some 80,000 kilometres of paved roads connected the provinces with Rome, built by legionaries for troops, messengers, and merchants. Aqueducts carried water over dozens of kilometres into the cities, and concrete made from volcanic ash allowed domes such as that of the Pantheon and harbour structures built under water. Water wheels, cranes, underfloor heating, and glass windows belonged to the state of the art; Hadrian's Wall and the limes showed how engineering secured frontiers.

In the 3rd century this system partly broke down: emperors reduced the silver content of the coinage in order to pay soldiers, prices exploded, and trade and cities suffered from civil wars and invasions. In 301 Diocletian tried in vain to impose maximum prices, and he bound peasants and craftsmen to their occupations. In the West the economy shifted to large estates, whose dependent coloni later became the peasants of the Middle Ages.

title: The Empires of Asia: Persia, India, China, Japan
summary: While Greeks and Romans ruled in Europe, great empires, world religions, and inventions such as paper and the compass arose in Asia and shape the world to this day.
overview: Around 550 BC Cyrus II united the Persians and the Medes and within a few decades created the largest empire in history up to that time. It reached from the Aegean to the Indus and was held together by satrapies, royal roads, and a policy of religious tolerance. In 330 BC Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire, yet Persian culture and administration lived on in the succeeding empires of the Parthians and the Sasanians.

At the same time new teachings arose in India and China that determine Asian thought to this day. Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught a way to overcome suffering in northern India, while Confucius in China devised an ethics of duty, education, and order. The Maurya king Ashoka made Buddhism the religion of a great empire in the 3rd century BC and sent missionaries as far as Sri Lanka.

In China, Qin Shi Huangdi ended the period of the Warring States in 221 BC and created a unified empire with a common script, currency, and system of measures. The succeeding Han dynasty ruled for four centuries, opened the Silk Road to the West, and raised Confucianism to the status of state doctrine. Under the Han, paper, the compass, and an administration of officials filled by examination also came into being.

Under the Gupta dynasty in the 4th and 5th centuries India experienced a golden age of mathematics, astronomy, poetry, and art; it was here that the decimal system with zero arose. Under the Tang dynasty from 618 onwards China reached a new peak: the capital Chang'an was the largest city in the world, and trade and Buddhism connected China with Central Asia, Korea, and Japan.

Japan adopted writing, Buddhism, and administration from China and, in the Heian period from 794, developed a courtly culture of its own with a syllabic script and novels. In Southeast Asia the Khmer built Angkor Wat, the largest temple complex in the world, in the 12th century. In this period the empires of Asia were often larger, richer, and technically more advanced than those of Europe.
consequences: Buddhism, Confucianism, and Hinduism still shape the religion, ethics, and society of billions of people in Asia.
China's unification under Qin Shi Huangdi created the basis for a state that endured for more than two thousand years despite many changes of dynasty.
Paper, the compass, gunpowder, and printing travelled from China westwards along the Silk Road and changed science, warfare, and education worldwide.
The Indian decimal system with zero was transmitted to Europe through the Arab world and is the basis of our mathematics today.
The Persian model of a multi-ethnic empire with provinces, roads, and religious tolerance influenced Alexander, Rome, and the later Islamic empires.
keyFacts: Around 500 BC Buddhism, Confucianism, and Daoism emerge, three teachings that shape Asian thought to this day.
In 221 BC Qin Shi Huangdi unifies China; his Terracotta Army, discovered in 1974, numbers around 8,000 clay soldiers.
Around 100 BC Sima Qian completes the Shiji, the first comprehensive work of Chinese historical writing.
In 224 Ardashir I founds the Sasanian Empire, which rules Persia until the Arab conquest in 651.
From 690 to 705 Wu Zetian reigns as the only woman in the history of China to rule as empress in her own right.
In 868 the Diamond Sutra is produced, the oldest surviving printed book bearing a date.
Around 1008 the lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu completes the Tale of Genji in Japan, the first novel in world literature.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The Chinese emperors justified their rule with the Mandate of Heaven: a just ruler governs with divine approval, an unjust one loses it and may be overthrown. Natural disasters, famines, and revolts were therefore regarded as warning signs from Heaven. This way of thinking explained why dynasties such as the Qin, the Han, or the Tang rose and fell again, and it allowed every successful rebel to present himself as the new bearer of the mandate. Even Wu Zetian, the only empress in her own right, had her rule confirmed by Buddhist scriptures and omens.

Unlike the aristocratic states of Europe, China had relied since the Han on a body of officials selected through examinations on the Confucian classics. Under the Tang, and especially under Wu Zetian, this system was extended, so that men from more modest families could also rise to high office. The officials administered taxes, granaries, canals, and courts in the provinces and were transferred regularly so that they could not build up a power base of their own. The model was adopted by Korea, Japan, and Vietnam.

In Persia the Sasanian kings ruled as Kings of Kings over a multi-ethnic empire in which the nobility, the Zoroastrian priests, and the warriors were separated by estate. Their permanent conflict with Rome and Byzantium over Armenia and Mesopotamia so exhausted both sides in the 7th century that the Arab armies had an easy task. In India, by contrast, great empires such as the Maurya, the Gupta, and the Chola remained exceptions; mostly numerous regional kings shared power, though the Chola in the south also ruled across the sea with a fleet.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The great majority of people lived in the countryside from growing rice and millet. In China the family, headed by the father, stood at the centre, and the veneration of ancestors connected the living with the dead. The state demanded from the peasants taxes in grain and cloth as well as labour service, with which walls, canals, and palaces were built. Those who could no longer render these dues fled or joined revolts, which several times brought down entire dynasties.

In India the caste system ordered society by birth into priests, warriors, peasants and merchants, and servants; below them stood the so-called untouchables. Buddhists and Jains rejected this order of rank, and in the monasteries people of all origins lived together. Women in the early civilizations of Asia mostly had limited rights, but there were exceptions: Buddhist nuns, learned ladies-in-waiting in Japan, and rulers such as Wu Zetian show that education and power were not reserved for men alone.

The cities of Asia far surpassed those of Europe in size. Chang'an, the capital of the Tang, was laid out on a grid, surrounded by walls, and divided into quarters with a night-time curfew; in its two great markets Persians, Sogdians, Indians, and Arabs traded. Teahouses, theatres, and temple festivals shaped city life, and with tea, which became the popular drink under the Tang, a distinct culture of enjoyment arose.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: Alongside Confucianism, Daoism arose in China, the way of non-action in harmony with nature ascribed to Laozi. The two teachings complemented each other: an official was a Confucian while in office and a Daoist in retirement. Buddhism was added by way of the Silk Road and became the third great teaching through monasteries, cave temples such as Longmen and Dunhuang, and pilgrims such as Xuanzang, who brought Indian scriptures to China. From China it spread to Korea and, in the 6th century, to Japan.

Persia was the home of Zoroastrianism with its struggle between good and evil, which influenced Christianity, Judaism, and Islam. Under the Sasanians the teaching of Zarathustra became the state religion; at the same time Jews, Christians, and Manichaeans lived in the empire, and the academy of Gundeshapur collected Greek and Indian knowledge. In India Sanskrit poetry, astronomy, and mathematics flourished; the dramas of Kalidasa and the calculations of Aryabhata are among the high points of the Gupta period.

In China historical writing attained a standing under Sima Qian that it had nowhere else in antiquity: every dynasty had the history of its predecessor written, and the archives of the court reach back to the Han period. The invention of woodblock printing in the 7th or 8th century made Buddhist sutras, calendars, and later the Confucian classics available in large numbers. In Japan ladies-in-waiting such as Murasaki Shikibu and Sei Shonagon created new literary forms, the novel and the diary, in the Japanese syllabic script.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The Silk Road was not a single route but a network of caravan routes and sea lanes connecting China, India, Persia, and the Mediterranean. Silk, lacquer, porcelain, and paper travelled westwards, and glass, horses, spices, precious stones, and silver eastwards; intermediaries such as the Sogdians in Samarkand and the Kushan Empire in Central Asia grew rich. Religions, diseases, and inventions travelled with the goods, and the harbours of southern India and Southeast Asia linked the network with maritime trade across the Indian Ocean.

For centuries China was the technically leading region of the world. Cast iron, the wheelbarrow, the stirrup, the seismograph, paper, the compass, and woodblock printing originated here long before Europe. Under the Song dynasty gunpowder weapons, paper money, movable type, and huge blast furnaces were added, and Kaifeng became a city of a million people with trading companies and exchange houses. The Chinese built canals such as the Grand Canal, which connected northern and southern China and secured the rice supply of the capitals.

India exported cotton fabrics, pepper, and precious stones and received Roman gold in return, as thousands of coin finds in the south attest. Steel production in southern India supplied the famous wootz steel, from which Damascus blades were later forged. Persia controlled the trade between East and West, minted silver coins that reached as far as China and Scandinavia, and developed an irrigation technique with underground channels, the qanats, that is still in use today.

title: The European Middle Ages
summary: Between the end of Rome and the discovery of America, Christianity, feudalism, knights, monasteries, and rising cities shaped a new Europe, while the Mongols, Mali, and the Aztecs established great empires of their own.
overview: After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Germanic kingdoms arose on its soil. The most successful were the Franks: their king Clovis was baptized a Catholic around 498 and thereby won the support of the church and of the Romance population. Charlemagne extended the Frankish kingdom as far as Saxony, Italy, and Spain and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800; his reign is regarded as the birth of medieval Europe.

The High Middle Ages from the 11th to the 13th century were a period of growth. The population increased, forests were cleared, cities were founded, and cathedrals were built. Society was divided into estates: the nobility fought, the clergy prayed, the peasants worked. Through feudalism the king bound dukes and counts to himself, and they owed him loyalty and military service in return. Monasteries preserved the knowledge of antiquity, and from 1088 the first universities arose in Bologna, Paris, and Oxford.

The Crusades from 1096 brought Europe into close and often violent contact with the Islamic world, but also promoted trade and the exchange of knowledge. From 793 the Vikings from Scandinavia plundered monasteries and coasts, founded cities such as Dublin and Kiev, and reached Greenland and North America. Their descendants, the Normans, conquered England in 1066. With the Magna Carta of 1215 kings had for the first time to acknowledge the rights of their subjects in writing.

Powerful empires arose outside Europe as well: from 1206 Genghis Khan created the largest contiguous land empire in history, which allowed merchants such as Marco Polo to travel as far as China. In Mali in West Africa the gold-rich king Mansa Musa impressed the entire Islamic world on his pilgrimage in 1324, and in Mexico the Aztecs founded their capital Tenochtitlan around 1325.

The Late Middle Ages were marked by crises. From 1347 the Black Death killed about a third of the European population, the Hundred Years' War devastated France, and famines and revolts shook the established order. In 1453 the Ottomans conquered Constantinople. At the same time printing, long-distance trade, and a new interest in antiquity were already announcing the modern age.
consequences: Christianity and the church shaped the law, education, calendar, and everyday life of Europe into the modern age; monasteries and universities became centres of knowledge.
France and the Holy Roman Empire emerged from the Frankish kingdom, and many of today's European states, cities, and borders have medieval roots.
The Magna Carta and municipal charters established the idea that rulers too are bound by laws; out of this parliaments and civil rights developed.
The Crusades, the Mongol Empire, and long-distance trade connected Europe with Asia and Africa and carried knowledge, goods, and diseases such as the plague across continents.
The crises of the 14th century weakened the nobility and serfdom, strengthened the cities and wage labour, and prepared the ground for the Renaissance and the Reformation.
keyFacts: In 529 Benedict of Nursia founds the monastery of Monte Cassino; his rule shapes Western monasticism.
In 537 the emperor Justinian consecrates the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, the largest church in Christendom for almost a thousand years.
In 843 the Treaty of Verdun divides the Frankish kingdom; out of West and East Francia arise France and Germany.
In 1077 King Henry IV asks the pope for forgiveness at Canossa: the climax of the Investiture Controversy between emperor and pope.
In 1088 the first university in Europe is founded in Bologna, and around 1140 Saint-Denis becomes the first Gothic church.
From about 1200 to 1450 Great Zimbabwe flourishes in southern Africa; from 1438 Pachacuti builds up the Inca Empire in the Andes.
In 1356 the Hanseatic cities meet in Lübeck for the first Hanseatic Diet; in 1381 the great Peasants' Revolt breaks out in England.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: Medieval kings did not rule from a capital but travelled with their court from palatinate to palatinate and from monastery to monastery in order to show their presence in the land. Their power rested on feudalism: the king granted land and offices to dukes, counts, and bishops, who owed him loyalty, counsel, and military service in return and who in turn passed land on to knights. In the eastern part of the Frankish kingdom the dukes elected the king from 911 onwards, and with Otto I an imperial office arose that understood itself as the successor of Rome and of Charlemagne and that used the bishops as a support of its rule.

The dispute over who was entitled to appoint bishops led in the 11th century to the Investiture Controversy between emperor and pope, which was only partly settled by Henry IV's penitential journey to Canossa in 1077 and the Concordat of Worms in 1122. From then on the popes claimed supremacy over all rulers, called for crusades, and waged a struggle over Italy lasting decades with the Hohenstaufen such as Frederick II. In the Holy Roman Empire the princes thereby gained in independence, while in France and England the kings centralized their power.

Outside Europe empires took other paths: under Justinian the Byzantine imperial office combined Roman law, the Greek language, and the Orthodox faith; in 988, with the baptism of Vladimir, Kievan Rus adopted Christianity and writing from Byzantium. In the Andes the Inca under Pachacuti created a state that administered millions of people without writing or wheels, by means of roads, storehouses, and knotted cords. In Africa rulers such as those of Great Zimbabwe and Mali controlled the trade in gold and ivory and built their power upon it.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: About nine out of ten people lived as peasants, many of them as serfs who paid dues to the lord of the manor and performed compulsory labour. Village life followed the church year and the seasons; from the 11th century the three-field system, the heavy wheeled plough, and the horse collar for draught horses increased yields. Crop failures nevertheless led again and again to famines, and life expectancy was far below that of today. After the Black Death labour became scarce, and peasants demanded freedom and better conditions, as in England in 1381.

In the cities a new society of merchants, craftsmen, and day labourers arose, who escaped serfdom after a year according to the principle that city air makes you free. Guilds regulated the training, prices, and quality of the crafts, and the city council, usually dominated by rich merchant families, negotiated with kings and princes. Women ran workshops and shops, worked in the textile and brewing trades, and in cities such as Cologne even appeared as guilds of their own. Jews lived in separate quarters, were excluded from the crafts, and were repeatedly exposed to persecution.

The nobility lived in castles and defined itself through arms, hunting, and the tournament; the ideal of the knight combined bravery with piety and courtly manners. At courts such as that of Eleanor of Aquitaine, troubadours and minnesingers sang of love and created a poetry in the vernacular languages. Monasteries took in the sons and daughters of the nobility, cared for the sick and the poor, and offered women such as Hildegard of Bingen a space for education and influence.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: The church pervaded every sphere of life: baptism, marriage, and burial, feast days, fasting, and the tithe determined the year, and the fear of hell and purgatory shaped people's thinking. The Rule of Benedict made monasteries places of prayer, work, and learning, whose scriptoria copied the texts of antiquity. In the 13th century Franciscans and Dominicans entered the cities and preached poverty, while pilgrims travelled to Santiago, Rome, and Jerusalem and relics were venerated. Byzantium and Kiev followed the Orthodox faith, which separated definitively from Rome in 1054.

With the universities of Bologna, Paris, and Oxford, a new type of place of learning arose from the 11th century onwards, in which law, theology, medicine, and the seven liberal arts were taught. Scholasticism sought to ground faith in reason; to this end Thomas Aquinas combined the philosophy of Aristotle, rediscovered through Arabic translations, with Christian doctrine. At the same time poetry flourished in the vernacular languages, from the Nibelungenlied through Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival to Dante's Divine Comedy.

Architecture reflected this new departure: the massive Romanesque churches with thick walls were followed from 1140 by the Gothic cathedrals, whose pointed arches, buttresses, and coloured glass windows let light into the interior as an image of God. Music was written down in notation for the first time, and polyphony developed in Paris. Outside Europe the builders of Great Zimbabwe raised walls metres high without mortar, and in Cusco and Machu Picchu the Inca fitted stones together so precisely that no knife blade fits between them.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: From the 11th to the 13th century the population of Europe doubled; forests were cleared, marshes drained, and settlers recruited as far as Eastern Europe. Water mills and windmills replaced manual labour in grinding, fulling, and sawing, and in the mines of the Harz and the Ore Mountains silver was extracted, which set coinage going again. Fairs in Champagne and later in Frankfurt and Geneva connected the merchants of Italy with those of Flanders and Germany.

Long-distance trade organized itself in leagues: around 1356 the Hanseatic League linked some 200 cities from London to Novgorod and traded in cloth, furs, wax, herring, and salt on its rounded cogs. Italian cities such as Venice and Genoa dominated Mediterranean trade in spices and silk from the East and developed bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping, and banks; the church forbade interest, but the merchants found ways to circumvent this prohibition. In Africa, caravans across the Sahara and harbours on the Swahili coast connected goldfields and sources of ivory with Cairo, India, and China.

Technical innovations changed everyday life and warfare: the mechanical clock, invented around 1300, divided the day into hours of equal length for the first time and struck from the towers of the cities. Papermaking, which came from China by way of the Arabs, as well as spectacles, the stirrup, and the crossbow spread, and around 1320 the first cannon appeared in Europe. In the Andes the Inca built terraced fields, suspension bridges, and a road network of more than 30,000 kilometres without iron or the wheel, on which runners carried messages and supplies.

title: The Islamic World
summary: Out of the message of Muhammad an empire arose within a century that reached from Spain to India, and whose scholars in Baghdad, Córdoba, and Cairo brought science, medicine, and philosophy to a new flowering.
overview: Around 610 Muhammad, a merchant from Mecca, began to proclaim to his fellow men revelations that, according to Islamic belief, he had received from God. His message of the one God, of social justice, and of the Last Judgement met with resistance in Mecca, so that in 622 he emigrated to Medina. There the first Muslim community arose; with this emigration, the Hijra, the Islamic calendar begins. By his death in 632 most of the tribes of Arabia had joined Islam.

Under the first caliphs, Arab armies conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Persia, and North Africa in an astonishingly short time. From 661 the Umayyads ruled from Damascus over an empire that by 711 also included Spain and parts of Central Asia; their expansion westwards was halted in 732 at Tours and Poitiers. Christians and Jews lived as protected subjects under Islamic rule; they paid a special tax but were allowed to keep their religion.

In 750 the Abbasids replaced the Umayyads and in 762 founded Baghdad, which soon became the largest city in the world. Under caliphs such as Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun, science flourished in the House of Wisdom: Greek, Persian, and Indian works were translated into Arabic, and scholars such as al-Khwarizmi, al-Razi, and Ibn Sina laid the foundations of algebra, astronomy, and medicine. The Muslims adopted the numerals with zero from India and papermaking from China.

Politically the caliphate fell apart: in Spain the Umayyads proclaimed a caliphate of their own in Córdoba in 929, in Egypt the Fatimids ruled, and Turkish sultans took power in the East. From 1096 the Crusades brought war with the Europeans; Saladin reconquered Jerusalem in 1187. In 1258 the Mongols destroyed Baghdad and put an end to the caliphate of the Abbasids.

Despite this catastrophe the Islamic world remained a connected cultural sphere in which travellers such as Ibn Battuta encountered fellow believers, mosques, and Arabic-speaking scholars everywhere from Morocco to China. Trade across the Sahara, the Indian Ocean, and the Silk Road spread Islam as far as West Africa, India, and Indonesia. Around 1300 the empire of the Ottomans arose in Anatolia, which conquered Constantinople in 1453 and became the new great power.
consequences: Islam became a world religion with almost two billion believers today and shapes the culture, law, and everyday life from Morocco to Indonesia.
Arab scholars preserved and extended the knowledge of antiquity; through translations from Toledo and Sicily, algebra, medicine, astronomy, and the philosophy of Aristotle reached Europe.
The Arabic numerals adopted from India, paper, and numerous words such as algebra, sugar, coffee, or cipher are part of the European heritage.
Muslim trade networks connected three continents and carried goods, plants such as sugar cane and oranges, and techniques such as irrigation and windmills over vast areas.
The conflicts of the Crusades and the conquest of Constantinople shaped the relationship between Europe and the Islamic world up to the present day.
keyFacts: In 624 the young Muslim community wins its first victory at Badr; in 680 the death of Husayn at Karbala deepens the separation of Sunnis and Shiites.
From 717 to 718 the great Arab siege of Constantinople fails; in 750 the Abbasid revolution overthrows the Umayyads.

Around 820 al-Khwarizmi founds algebra in Baghdad with his book on calculation; in 859 Fatima al-Fihri endows the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez, one of the oldest institutions of higher learning in the world.
In 969 the Fatimids found Cairo and in 970 the al-Azhar mosque, which still exists today as a place of learning.
In 1071 the Seljuks defeat Byzantium at Manzikert and open Anatolia to Turkish settlers.

In the 12th century Ibn Rushd expounds the works of Aristotle in Córdoba and thereby shapes the thinking of the European universities; in the 14th century Timbuktu and the Alhambra become emblems of Islamic scholarship and art.
From 1370 to 1405 Timur conquers an empire from Delhi to Ankara; in 1492 the fall of Granada ends almost 800 years of Muslim rule in Spain.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: After Muhammad's death in 632, four caliphs from his closest circle took over the leadership of the community; Muslims call them the rightly guided caliphs. Even in this period the dispute over the legitimate succession broke out: the followers of Ali, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet, regarded the leadership as a matter for his family, while the majority held the election of the most suitable man to be right. Out of this conflict the Shiites and the Sunnis emerged, and the struggles from 656 to 661 as well as the death of Husayn at Karbala in 680 became founding narratives of both branches.

The caliphs of the Umayyads and the Abbasids understood themselves as successors of the Prophet with religious and worldly authority, but in fact governed with administrations shaped by Persian practice, with viziers, tax registers, and postal routes. From the 9th century onwards provinces broke away under dynasties of their own: the Aghlabids and Fatimids in North Africa, the Samanids and Buyids in Persia, the Umayyads in Spain. The caliph in Baghdad remained a spiritual head whose name was mentioned in the Friday prayer, while Turkish military slaves and later the Seljuks exercised actual power.

From the 11th century the sultan, the holder of power in the name of the caliph, became the typical ruling figure of the Islamic world. The Seljuks, the Ayyubids of Saladin, the Mamluks in Egypt, and finally the Ottomans relied on cavalry armies, military slaves, and the revenues from land that they granted to their officers. Conquerors such as the Mongols and Timur destroyed cities and irrigation systems, but soon adopted Islam themselves and supported scholars and master builders at their courts.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: The cities were the heart of the Islamic world: around the Friday mosque lay the bazaar with its lanes arranged by trade, the caravanserai for merchants, baths, fountains, and residential quarters with inner courtyards. Cairo, Baghdad, Damascus, and Córdoba were among the largest cities of their time, supplied by irrigated fields, granaries, and a network of long-distance roads. In the countryside peasants lived in villages under landlords, alongside nomads who bred camels, sheep, and horses and who protected caravans or raided them.

Religion shaped the course of the day with five prayers, the fasting month of Ramadan, the prohibition of wine and pork, and the alms tax for the poor. Christians, Jews, and Zoroastrians lived as protected subjects with their own communities, courts, and houses of worship, but had to pay a poll tax and were mostly excluded from high office; in al-Andalus and Baghdad Jewish physicians, viziers, and scholars nevertheless rose to prominence. Slavery was widespread; slaves from Africa, the Caucasus, and the steppes served in households, armies, and palaces, and military slaves such as the Mamluks could rise as far as rulership.

Women were legally disadvantaged, but received shares of inheritance, could own property, and could establish endowments. Aisha, the wife of the Prophet, transmitted hundreds of sayings of Muhammad and taught in Medina, Fatima al-Fihri endowed a mosque with a college in Fez, and rulers such as Shajar al-Durr in Egypt or Raziyya in Delhi governed in their own right for a time. In poems, travel accounts, and legal documents women appear as merchants, poets, mystics, and scholars.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: In the 8th and 9th centuries the foundations of the Islamic religious sciences were laid: scholars collected and examined the hadiths, the transmitted sayings of the Prophet, and developed four Sunni schools of law from them. Alongside legal scholarship, the mysticism of Sufism flourished, which strove for immediate experience of God; Rabia of Basra, al-Ghazali, and Rumi joined it with poetry and philosophy, and Sufi brotherhoods carried Islam to India, Anatolia, and Africa.

The translation movement of Baghdad laid the ground for centuries of original research. Al-Khwarizmi created algebra, al-Biruni calculated the radius of the earth, Ibn al-Haytham founded optics on experiments, al-Razi and Ibn Sina wrote medical textbooks, and observatories were built in Maragha and Samarkand. Philosophers such as al-Farabi and Ibn Rushd interpreted Aristotle anew; from the 13th century their Latin translations from Toledo determined the curriculum of the universities from Paris to Padua. In the 14th century Ibn Khaldun devised a theory of the rise and fall of empires that is regarded as the beginning of the social sciences.

Because pictorial representations were avoided in mosques, artists brought calligraphy, geometric ornament, and the arabesque to the highest perfection. Mosques with domes, minarets, and prayer niches, palace cities such as the Alhambra, manuscripts of the Quran, miniature painting from Persia, and carpets from Anatolia show the variety of the art. Poetry was the most esteemed art; the Persian epics of Ferdowsi, the quatrains of Omar Khayyam, and the love poetry of Hafez are still read today.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: The Islamic world lay at the intersection of the trade routes of three continents. Caravans brought gold and slaves from West Africa across the Sahara to North Africa, ships sailed with the monsoon from Basra and Aden to India, East Africa, and China, and the Silk Road connected Baghdad by way of Samarkand with the Far East. A common language, Islamic law, and the gold dinar made business over thousands of kilometres easier; merchants used bills of exchange, credit, and trading companies long before these became customary in Italy.

Agriculture and technology were advanced by the farmers and engineers of the Near East: water wheels, underground channels, and cisterns irrigated fields from Persia to Spain, where rice, sugar cane, cotton, oranges, and lemons were grown. From the 8th century paper mills were established in Samarkand and Baghdad and made libraries, administration, and the book trade possible. Scholars such as al-Jazari described pumps, water clocks, and automata, and from Damascus and Toledo came famous blades, glassware, and ceramics.

The wealth of the cities depended on safe trade routes and intact irrigation systems. The devastation wrought by the Mongols in the 13th century and by Timur in the 14th, the plague from 1347, and the shift of trade to the sea routes of the Europeans from 1500 hit the old centres hard. At the same time new areas flourished: Timbuktu and Gao on the Niger, Kilwa and Zanzibar on the East African coast, Malacca in Southeast Asia, and the rising Ottoman Empire with Bursa and later Istanbul.

title: Renaissance, Discoveries, and Reformation
summary: Between 1400 and 1600, printing, humanism, the voyages to America and India, and the division of the church change Europe's view of the world and connect the continents permanently for the first time.
overview: In the 15th century scholars and artists in the Italian city-states such as Florence, Venice, and Rome turned once again to antiquity. This rebirth, the Renaissance, placed the human being and his abilities at the centre. Rich banking families such as the Medici supported painters, sculptors, and architects, and humanism spread a new form of education based on Greek and Latin sources. Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raphael created works that are still regarded today as high points of European art.

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz developed printing with movable metal type. Books thereby became cheaper and quicker to produce, and knowledge spread at a pace previously unknown. Pamphlets, Bibles in the vernacular, and scientific works now reached a broad public. Without printing neither the Reformation nor the new natural science would have advanced so rapidly.

At the same time Portuguese and Spanish seafarers sought new routes to the spices and the gold of Asia. Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, Vasco da Gama India in 1498, and between 1519 and 1522 Magellan's fleet circumnavigated the earth for the first time. Spanish conquerors under Cortés and Pizarro destroyed the empires of the Aztecs and the Inca. For the population of the Americas the arrival of the Europeans meant disease, violence, and forced labour; millions of people died, and from the 16th century Africans were carried across the Atlantic as slaves.

In 1517 the monk Martin Luther published his 95 Theses against the trade in indulgences. What began as a call for reform of the church led to the division of Western Christendom into Catholics and Protestants. Princes, cities, and peasants used the new teaching for their own ends, and Europe was plunged into wars of religion. The Catholic Church responded to the challenge with the Council of Trent and the Jesuit order.

The picture of the cosmos was also set in motion. In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus placed the sun instead of the earth at the centre of the universe, and observation and mathematics gradually took the place of the old authorities. At the end of the 16th century Europe was wealthier, better educated, and at the same time more deeply divided than ever before, and its ships connected all the inhabited continents for the first time.
consequences: Printing made knowledge available on a mass scale and created the basis for a public sphere, science, and modern education.
The voyages of discovery joined Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas into a worldwide trading network; plants, animals, diseases, and people were exchanged between the continents.
The conquest of the Americas destroyed the indigenous empires and established centuries of colonial rule as well as the transatlantic slave trade.
The Reformation divided Christendom permanently, strengthened the territorial princes, and set off wars of religion that lasted until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
The Renaissance and the heliocentric view of the world placed the human being, reason, and observation at the centre and prepared the way for the scientific revolution and the Enlightenment.
keyFacts: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invents printing with movable type in Mainz; by 1500 some 30,000 titles have been printed in Europe.
In 1492 Columbus reaches the Caribbean; in 1494 Spain and Portugal divide the non-European world between them in the Treaty of Tordesillas.
In 1517 Luther sets off the Reformation with the 95 Theses, in 1521 he refuses to recant at Worms, and in 1555 the Peace of Augsburg recognizes two confessions in the empire.
In 1543 the heliocentric world view of Copernicus and the anatomy of Vesalius appear in the same year, two cornerstones of modern natural science.
The Ottoman Empire under Suleiman, the Mughal Empire under Akbar, and the Songhai Empire in West Africa are among the most powerful states of the age.
In 1588 the Spanish Armada fails off England; in 1582 Pope Gregory XIII introduces the calendar still in use today.
Between 1500 and 1600 European traders already carry off hundreds of thousands of Africans to the Americas as slaves.

sections.title: Rule and Politics
paragraphs: The Italian city-states were the political laboratory of the Renaissance. In Florence the Medici banking family governed from 1434 onwards without crown or title, by skilfully steering offices, elections, and patronage. Venice remained an aristocratic republic with an elected doge, Milan was ruled by dukes, and the pope was at the same time the sovereign of the Papal States. In 1513, in The Prince, Niccolò Machiavelli described soberly how power is won and maintained, and thereby founded modern political thought.

North of the Alps large monarchies grew together. Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon united Spain and completed the Reconquista in 1492 with the conquest of Granada. From 1519 their grandson Charles V united Spain, the Netherlands, Naples, Austria, and the imperial crown and ruled an empire on which the sun never set. France and England consolidated their royal power; in 1534 Henry VIII detached the English church from Rome and made himself its head.

The Reformation became a question of power. Territorial princes such as Electoral Saxony and Hesse used the new teaching to take over church property and authority over the church, and joined together in the Schmalkaldic League in 1531. After war and negotiation, the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 laid down that each territorial ruler determined the confession of his territory. In France, by contrast, the conflict led to eight wars of religion, whose climax was the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572.

sections.title: Society and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Around 1500 Europe was a society of peasants. About nine out of ten people lived in the countryside, paid dues to landlords and to the church, and in many places were serfs. The population grew again after the plague years, grain prices rose, and the Twelve Articles of the peasants of 1525 show how strongly the rural population felt threatened by new burdens. At the same time the potato, maize, the tomato, and the turkey from the Americas brought new foodstuffs to Europe in the long run.

In the cities, guilds, councils, and patrician families determined life. Craftsmen, merchants, and scholars formed a self-confident bourgeoisie that bought books, endowed schools, and had portraits of themselves painted. Women helped to run households and workshops, but were excluded from the universities and from most guilds; exceptions such as the painter Sofonisba Anguissola or the Reformation writer Argula von Grumbach remained rare. The witch trials, which increased towards the end of the 16th century, affected predominantly women.

For the peoples of the Americas and Africa the age of discoveries meant catastrophe. Smallpox, measles, and influenza, against which the indigenous population had no defences, killed the greater part of the inhabitants of Central and South America within a century. The Spanish system of the encomienda forced survivors to work in mines and on plantations. The Dominican Bartolomé de Las Casas denounced the atrocities and obtained protective laws in 1542, which however were scarcely enforced.

sections.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
paragraphs: Humanism was the educational movement of the age. Scholars such as Erasmus of Rotterdam sought in Greek and Latin manuscripts the unadulterated text of antiquity and of the Bible, mocked scholastic hair-splitting, and called for an educated, peaceable Christendom. Greek and Hebrew were taught at the universities, and Erasmus's Greek New Testament of 1516 became the basis for Luther's translation. Printing transformed this scholarly culture into a public debate with pamphlets, satirical prints, and songs.

In art, painters and sculptors sought the laws of nature. Brunelleschi discovered central perspective, Leonardo studied muscles and tendons on corpses, and between 1508 and 1512 Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. North of the Alps, Albrecht Dürer, Hans Holbein, and Pieter Bruegel created works that captured landscape, everyday life, and the portrait in new ways. Towards the end of the century the theatre flourished in London, and William Shakespeare wrote plays that are still performed worldwide today.

Natural research began to replace authorities with observation. In 1543 Andreas Vesalius corrected the anatomy handed down since Galen through dissections of his own, in the same year Copernicus set the earth in motion, and Tycho Brahe measured the heavens with hitherto unequalled precision. The calendar reform of 1582 showed how astronomy and the church could work together. At the same time the church defended its doctrine with the Index, the Inquisition, and the new Jesuit order, which founded schools throughout Europe and in the mission territories.

sections.title: Economy and Technology
paragraphs: Trading houses and banks shaped the economy. The Medici in Florence and the Fuggers in Augsburg financed popes and emperors; in 1519 Jakob Fugger paid for the election of Charles V and controlled copper and silver mining in Tyrol and Hungary. Bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping, and networks of branches made financial transactions over great distances possible. Antwerp replaced Bruges and Venice as the most important trading centre of north-western Europe.

The voyages of discovery rested on new technology. The caravel with its triangular sails could tack against the wind, the compass, the astrolabe, and the cross-staff allowed position to be determined on the open sea, and Portuguese schools of navigation collected charts and experience. Heavy ship's guns gave European fleets superiority in the Indian Ocean. Spices, silk, and porcelain from Asia, as well as sugar from the new plantations of the Atlantic islands and Brazil, became the goods of world trade.

Silver flowed from the Americas to Europe. After the discovery of the mines of Potosí in 1545 and Zacatecas in 1546, hundreds of tonnes of silver arrived each year in Seville and went on to Genoa, Antwerp, and by way of Manila as far as China.
